title: The sabbath idea
hook: Judaism's weekly day of rest, rooted in creation and the commandments (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hadith on small, regular deeds. Your line was same time next week. Is it in the calendar? Day one hundred forty-three.

It's Friday, just before sunset, in a Jewish home. The cooking is done. The table is set. Someone lights two candles. In an observant home, phones go off and stay off. Until three stars appear on Saturday night, there will be no shopping, no work emails, no building anything. Just meals, prayer, walks, naps, conversation. The Torah commands it, and Jewish families have kept it, stopping the world like this week after week. A new week of our path starts here, with rest, and it starts with the original. Today's word is Shabbat.

Shabbat comes from a Hebrew root that means to stop, to cease. It goes back to the very first pages of the Torah. In Genesis, after six days of creation, God finishes the work, rests on the seventh day, and blesses it and makes it holy. Later, in the Ten Commandments, the command comes plainly: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." And it isn't only for the family. The text includes servants, animals and the stranger in town: everyone gets the day. The Torah gives two reasons, in two places. In Exodus, the reason is creation: God rested, so you rest. In Deuteronomy, the reason is freedom: remember you were slaves in Egypt, and slaves never get a day off. What counts as work? The rabbis of the Mishnah listed thirty-nine kinds, which rabbinic tradition ties to the tasks of building the sanctuary in the wilderness: sowing, baking, sewing, writing, building, kindling a fire. Notice what they share. They're all kinds of making. Shabbat is a day off from making: a day for living in the world instead of changing it. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described it as a palace built in time rather than in space. The Jewish Sabbath has its own laws, its own prayers and its own meaning, and it belongs to the Jewish people. This week, the path only borrows the idea underneath it, with respect: that a person needs a regular stretch where nothing has to be produced.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one rest window this week. Settle, and breathe. Look at the week ahead. Find a stretch, an evening, a morning, a few hours, where you could stop making things: no work, no errands, no fixing, no producing. Picture when it begins, maybe with a small sign, like switching off a lamp or a phone. Picture what you'll do instead: eat, walk, talk, nap. The bell holds the time.
Shabbat. Judaism's weekly day of rest, from a Hebrew root for stopping, kept from Friday sunset to Saturday night. Today's word.
Your line: a day off from making. Today, choose your rest window for this week, and tell one person when it is. Day one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Many Jews keep Shabbat from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall, lighting candles, sharing meals and prayer, and refraining from the kinds of work Jewish law describes; practice varies across Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and secular Jews.

original.note: Hebrew, Shabbat: the sabbath, from the root sh-b-t, to stop or cease.

trapdoor: what you thought: a day for going to synagogue.
what it means: a weekly day off from making, for everyone in the house, even the animals.
what a scholar hears: two reasons (Exodus 20, Deuteronomy 5), and the Mishnah's thirty-nine categories of work (Shabbat 7:2), tied to the Tabernacle.
